candidates.name: siloah-travel-mcp
candidates.what_it_holds: MCP server + REST API (mcp.siloah.travel) indexing 70,000+ cruise voyages, 678 ships, 62 cruise lines (20 active), 6,700+ ports, 11,000+ cabin types across 30 languages. No local data files committed — queries a live Postgres/Supabase+pgvector backend on Cloudflare Workers; supports filtering by destination, departure city, cruise line, duration, price. MIT licensed, 7 commits.
candidates.why_useful: A single free API surface that already aggregates cruise-line schedule/capacity breadth (ships, itineraries, ports) across 62 lines including NCLH/RCL/CCL brands — could be pulled repeatedly to build a point-in-time itinerary-count/capacity proxy for gap #18 (cruise book-ahead analogue) without scraping individual cruise-line sites.
candidates.time_coverage: current/live snapshot only (no historical vintages found)
candidates.size_hint: 70k voyages, 678 ships, 6.7k ports (live DB, not committed)

candidates.name: vessel-traffic-mcp
candidates.what_it_holds: Read-only MCP server normalizing vessel identity, AIS-style positions, port calls, and shipping schedules across a provider tier system: fixture data (deterministic test data, no network), public opt-in browser-captured adapters (MyShipTracking, Tradlinx, AIsFriends), and BYOK commercial APIs (MarineTraffic, VesselFinder, AISStream, AISHub, BarentsWatch, SeaRates, Routescanner, VesselAPI). No bulk data committed beyond test fixtures. MIT licensed, 101 commits.
candidates.why_useful: A generic client/normalizer for AIS-based port-call and vessel-schedule data; could in principle be pointed at a specific cruise ship's IMO/MMSI to derive port-dwell-time / itinerary-pace as an occupancy-timing proxy, but requires paid API keys (BYOK) for anything beyond fixtures, and explicitly avoids bypassing paywalls.

candidates.name: timonelo
candidates.what_it_holds: A 'cruise intelligence' knowledge-graph platform (Python/Pydantic backend, TypeScript/React frontend) organizing evidence about ships, cabins, routes and ports under knowledge/ships/, knowledge/evidence/ (SHA-256-verified artifacts), and data/hypotheses/ (explicitly quarantined, non-canonical). No dataset size/time-span documented; 230 commits on develop branch. MIT licensed.
candidates.why_useful: Early-stage structured schema for cruise ship/route/port facts with a verification discipline; not a ready dataset but worth watching if it accumulates a real corpus of route/capacity facts.

candidates.name: norwegian-cruise-line (API Evangelist profile)
candidates.what_it_holds: Independent third-party documentation profile of NCLH's public API surface (apis.yml/OpenAPI metadata, screenshots, security notes). Explicitly finds 'No public developer portal or external API offering has been identified for Norwegian Cruise Line Holdings' — GDS/travel-agent integrations only. No pricing, schedule, or operational data. 32 commits, last modified 2026-05-16.
candidates.why_useful: Confirms there is no public NCLH API to scrape/pull — useful negative result to record so nobody re-investigates this path, but holds no usable data itself.

candidates.name: royal-caribbean (API Evangelist profile)
candidates.what_it_holds: Same API Evangelist third-party profile format as the NCLH repo, covering Royal Caribbean Group (Royal Caribbean International, Celebrity Cruises, Silversea). Documentation/metadata only, no committed operational data. Last updated September 2026.
candidates.why_useful: Companion profile to the NCLH/Carnival ones; worth a one-line catalogue entry but no usable data found.

candidates.name: carnival-corporation (API Evangelist profile)
candidates.what_it_holds: Same API Evangelist format covering Carnival Corporation's eight cruise brands (Carnival, Princess, Holland America, etc.), including notes on OceanMedallion wearable platform and loyalty apps. Documentation/metadata only (apis.yml), no pricing/schedule data. Created 2026-05-05, last modified 2026-05-16.
candidates.why_useful: Confirms no public developer API surface for Carnival brands either; catalogue value only as a negative result / pointer to the OceanMedallion app ecosystem for future method ideas (app-store review mining, gap #14).

candidates.name: opentravel-alliance (API Evangelist profile)
candidates.what_it_holds: Profile of the OpenTravel Alliance standards body covering air/hospitality/car-rental/cruise/rail/GDS message specifications. Contains 8 harvested Swagger/OpenAPI docs and points to the upstream mirror github.com/OpenTravel/OpenTravel-Specifications, which the profile says holds 543 JSON Schema files (public OTA 1.0 tree stops at release 2017B; website offers releases through 2024A). No license file on this profiling repo. Last commit 2026-07-28 (creation); upstream mirror last updated 2024-11-26.
candidates.why_useful: Points to a real, larger upstream repo (OpenTravel/OpenTravel-Specifications) that defines the standard XML/JSON message formats used for cruise GDS booking/availability messages — a methods reference for anyone building a cruise-booking-API client, though not itself a dataset.
candidates.time_coverage: OTA 1.0 through 2017B (public mirror); commercial releases through 2024A not mirrored
candidates.license: royalty-free per OpenTravel Alliance (this profile repo has no LICENSE)

candidates.name: edgartools
candidates.what_it_holds: Python library (2.7k stars, 4,388 commits, MIT) that converts SEC EDGAR filings (10-K/10-Q/8-K, XBRL, insider trades, fund holdings, 20+ form types) into structured objects, e.g. Company('NCLH').get_facts().query().by_concept(...). No API key or subscription required; works for any US-listed ticker.
candidates.why_useful: General-purpose, no-cost way to pull point-in-time XBRL facts for NCLH/CCL/RCL — including custom tags cruise lines use for 'Advance ticket sales' / deferred revenue — quarter by quarter, which is exactly the book-ahead analogue metric gap #18 wants. Also usable for point-in-time company_filings_estimates work generally (gap #4).
candidates.time_coverage: as far back as each company's EDGAR XBRL history goes (typically 2009+)

candidates.name: SEC-XBRL-Financial-Statement-Dataset
candidates.what_it_holds: GitHub repo holds only SQL scripts (7 Athena table DDLs) and docs; the actual data is Parquet files in s3://dataset.secdatabase.com/sec_financial_statements/parquet/, covering Jan 2009–Sep 2020, ~12,600 companies, 239,700 annual/quarterly reports, 192.5M data points, 20GB+ compressed — full text and numeric XBRL financial-statement data (would include NCLH/CCL/RCL line items such as advance ticket sales / customer deposits for that window). 37 commits, no license stated.
candidates.why_useful: A bulk, queryable (Athena/Redshift Spectrum) historical XBRL financial-statement corpus stopping in 2020 — could backfill pre-2023 cruise-line advance-ticket-sales and deferred-revenue history as a book-ahead analogue baseline (gap #18) and as a general point-in-time financial-statement source (gap #4), though it requires AWS access and does not cover 2021-2026.
candidates.last_activity: 37 commits total, exact date not shown

candidates.name: phantomtide
candidates.what_it_holds: Global maritime intelligence platform for real-time vessel tracking, AIS data analysis, sanctions monitoring, shipping routes and port activity. 124 stars. Generic AIS-based tool, not cruise-specific; data comes from live AIS feeds, not a committed dataset.
candidates.why_useful: Could in theory be adapted to track specific cruise-ship IMO numbers for port-call frequency/dwell time as a very indirect capacity-utilization proxy, but it is a general OSINT maritime-intelligence tool with no cruise-specific data or documentation, and likely depends on paid AIS feeds for full coverage.

candidates.name: pyais
candidates.what_it_holds: Python library (254 stars) decoding AIS message formats (AIVDM/AIVDO) into vessel identification and position data. A decoder/parser only, no committed vessel data.
candidates.why_useful: Baseline tooling if the team ever wanted to build its own cruise-ship-position/port-call tracker from a raw AIS feed (e.g. AISHub free feed) rather than relying on a commercial API; general infrastructure only, several steps removed from any ABNB-relevant series today.

notes: Dead end on the intended modality: the shared WebSearch tool budget (200/200) was already exhausted session-wide before this scout ran any query, so no WebSearch calls returned results at all. Fallback to WebFetch against SERPs mostly failed too: github.com/search is rate-limited (HTTP 429, Retry-After 3600s) for this session/IP; DuckDuckGo (both html. and lite.) served CAPTCHA challenges; Google and Kaggle search pages are JS-rendered SPAs that return only an empty shell to a non-JS fetch; Bing rendered a real page but ignored the site: operator and returned generic commercial cruise-booking results with no github.com links in the visible snippet; Ecosia (403), Startpage (unsupported host), grep.app (429), Sourcegraph (403) were all blocked. The only reliable path was WebFetch directly against github.com/topics/<tag> pages, which do render server-side, plus direct WebFetch verification of specific repo pages found that way or guessed from prior knowledge (api-evangelist company profiles, dgunning/edgartools, secdatabase's SEC-XBRL dataset). Net result: there is no real committed 'cruise advance ticket sales / capacity / schedule' dataset on GitHub as such — the closest things are (a) a live cruise-voyage-index API/MCP server (Siloah), (b) generic AIS/vessel-tracking tooling that could theoretically be pointed at cruise-ship IMOs but needs paid feeds, and (c) generic SEC/XBRL tooling (edgartools, secdatabase's historical Parquet corpus) that can pull NCLH/CCL/RCL's actual 'advance ticket sales' and customer-deposit line items point-in-time — this last one is probably the highest-value, most concrete lead for gap #18's cruise book-ahead analogue, since it gets at real disclosed dollar figures rather than a proxy. Recommend a future scout retry github.com/search directly via `gh api` (not `gh search`, which other agents are using) once the 429 cooldown (~1hr from this run) has passed, and also try Similarweb/statista-adjacent free trackers or CLIA's own published 'State of the Cruise Industry' PDFs (not GitHub, but a primary source worth a non-GitHub scout) for actual passenger-volume and occupancy series.
